# Estimating the effect of pravastatin vs usual care under full adherence in the Antihypertensive and Lipid-Lowering Treatment to Prevent Heart Attack Trial—Lipid Lowering Trial

**Authors:** Rienna G. Russo; Anna Siefkas; Barry R. Davis; Eric B. Rimm; Issa J. Dahabreh; Miguel A. Hernán; Goodarz Danaei

**Affiliations:** 1CAUSALab, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States | 2Department of Epidemiology, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States | 3Coordinating Center for Clinical Trials, UTHealth Houston School of Public Health, Houston, TX, United States | 4Department of Nutrition, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States | 5Channing Division of Network Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | 6Department of Biostatistics, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States | 7Richard A. and Susan F. Smith Center for Outcomes Research, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | 8Department of Global Health and Populations, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States

## Abstract

The Antihypertensive and Lipid-Lowering Treatment to Prevent Heart Attack—Lipid-Lowering Trial (ALLHAT-LLT) was a pragmatic randomized trial conducted in 513 clinical centers across North America from 1994 to 2002. ALLHAT-LLT, which used standard of care (usual care) as the control treatment, did not find an effect of assignment to pravastatin on all-cause death. We aimed to use the trial data to estimate the effect of adhering to the assigned treatment, that is, the per-protocol effect. Moderately hypercholesterolemic (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol 100–189 mg/dL), hypertensive participants ≥55 years old were included and randomized to pravastatin (40 mg/day unless contraindicated) or usual care (lipid-lowering treatment discouraged unless clinically indicated). Of 10 355 individuals randomized, we included 9741 with complete baseline data. One-third of individuals in the pravastatin arm were non-adherent to the assigned treatment strategy at year 5. After adjusting for factors related to adherence, the 5 year risk difference comparing pravastatin to usual care was −3.0% (−4.9%, −1.3%), and the risk ratio was 0.79 (0.68, 0.91) for death. Findings were consistent across different definitions of treatment strategies. Our results suggest that the use of pravastatin under full adherence was protective against death, even if assignment to pravastatin was not clearly protective.

## Introduction

Current evidence favors the use of statins to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) and mortality,1,2 which makes the findings of the Antihypertensive and Lipid-Lowering Treatment to Prevent Heart Attack Trial—Lipid Lowering Trial (ALLHAT-LLT) an outlier.3 ALLHAT-LLT was a pragmatic, multi-center, unblinded, randomized trial of pravastatin (40 mg/day) vs usual care among moderately hypercholesterolemic, hypertensive participants.2 In contrast to other major statin trials that found benefits,4–6 in ALLHAT-LLT the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect, that is, the effect of assignment to treatment strategies, regardless of adherence to the assigned treatment strategies, on the primary outcome was widely interpreted as no difference in the risks of cardiovascular endpoints or death between the randomized treatment strategies.3

ALLHAT-LLT was a pragmatic trial in which treatment strategies were designed to accommodate the changing clinical circumstances of enrolled patients. Patients assigned to usual care were discouraged from taking lipid-lowering therapy unless clinically warranted. For example, if a patient had an elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) level, say, LDL-C ≥ 190 mg/dL, then they should have received lipid-lowering therapy according to the guidelines at that time (National Cholesterol Education Program (NCEP)’s Adult Treatment Panel II-III). Patients assigned to pravastatin were allowed to switch to other lipid-lowering treatments, or discontinue, if adverse effects occurred.

The per-protocol effect from randomized trials is also of interest to patients and clinicians. Learning about the effect of being assigned and adhering to the assigned strategies as defined in the protocol, that is, the per-protocol effect, may help elucidate reasons for null or attenuated intention-to-treat estimates, especially in pragmatic trials.7 Yet, per-protocol effects are often estimated post-hoc rather than as part of the pre-specified analyses, or using naïve approaches, such as restriction to the “per-protocol subset” of the trial or censoring of individuals when they discontinue treatment without adjusting for factors that drive treatment changes.8–10 The need to rely on assumptions for valid inference about per-protocol effects, beyond those justified by randomization, and analytic challenges in the presence of substantial non-adherence may contribute to the general reluctance in using per-protocol analyses to complement the intention-to-treat analyses of randomized trials.

Here, we re-analyze ALLHAT-LLT to demonstrate the added value of per-protocol analyses in pragmatic trials. We define non-adherence as deviations from treatment strategies based on the ALLHAT-LLT protocol and adjust for post-randomization factors that predict non-adherence to estimate the effect of pravastatin compared to usual care under full adherence on the 5 year risk of death and MACEs.11

## Methods

### The ALLHAT

ALLHAT-LLT was a randomized, unblinded trial, with enrollment from March 1994 to May 1998 and follow-up through March 2002 across 513 clinical centers in North America.3 Men and women aged 55 years and older were eligible for ALLHAT-LLT if they had stage 1 or 2 hypertension with at least 1 additional coronary heart disease risk factor; had a fasting LDL-C level of 100–189 mg/dL; and had fasting triglycerides <350 mg/dL. Individuals were excluded if they were currently receiving lipid-lowering therapy, were taking large doses of niacin, were taking probucol in the last year, were known to be intolerant of statins or have significant liver or kidney disease, had other contraindications for statin therapy, or had a secondary cause of hyperlipidemia. Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to (1) pravastatin, or (2) usual care, defined as:

- Pravastatin: Initiate 20 mg, increasing to 40 mg/day (maximum dose) as needed to achieve 25% reduction in LDL-C. Study clinicians have the option to lower the dose, discontinue the dose if serious side effects occur, or prescribe other lipid-lowering medications.

- Usual care: Treat according to the discretion of primary care clinicians, with lipid-lowering therapy discouraged unless prompted by a change in clinical circumstances. Circumstances may include LDL-C ≥ 190 mg/dL, incident cardiovascular events, or anything else deemed worthy of pharmaceutical intervention by the clinician.

Participants were followed from randomization until death or administrative end of follow-up. Follow-up was scheduled for 3, 6, 9, and 12 months post-randomization and then every 4 months. At study visits, participants were asked about the use of pravastatin, concurrent medications (including other statins and lipid-lowering therapies), and health behaviors. Participants discontinuing the study treatment were asked about reasons for discontinuation, which included “morbid event,” “symptomatic adverse event,” “other adverse effect (e.g., laboratory),” “non-medical reason,” and “refused to respond or unknown.”

Data on procedures and events that occurred since the prior visit were corroborated with hospital discharge summaries and death certificates, to verify the timing, procedure, diagnosis, or cause of death.

The primary outcome of the ALLHAT-LLT analysis plan was death from any cause. In addition, we investigated a composite outcome of MACEs, consisting of incident myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, and cardiovascular disease deaths, which had not been studied in the original trial. All cardiovascular events from the original trial were used; a random 10% subsample of these events had been adjudicated, and diagnoses based on hospitalization records were confirmed. Individuals were followed from randomization until they experienced an event, they were lost to follow-up (which we defined as ≥2 years between study visits), or the administrative end of follow-up, whichever happened first.

Additional details regarding the recruitment and randomization methods in ALLHAT-LLT have been published elsewhere.3 The trial protocol for ALLHAT-LLT is available in online supplementary materials (Supplemental Appendix). The trial protocol and data for ALLHAT-LLT are available upon request from the Biologic Specimen and Data Repository Information Coordinating Center (BioLINCC). The institutional review board of Harvard University approved the secondary data analysis.

### Causal contrasts

ALLHAT-LLT focused on the intention-to-treat effect. This effect is identifiable because exchangeability, consistency, and positivity are supported by aspects of the experimental design, including randomization. We specifically focused on the intention-to-treat effect, which we defined as the total effect for the cardiovascular outcome, including the effects of assignment through the competing event of non-cardiovascular death.12

In this paper, we also investigated the per-protocol effect. Because estimation of the per-protocol effect was not part of the original trial’s protocol,11 the characterization of the treatment strategies of interest is, to some extent, subject to interpretation because the trial protocol left some treatment decisions up to the clinician. We therefore defined a set of possible treatment strategies that tailor treatment to changing patient characteristics to varying degrees. In the primary analysis, the pravastatin strategy required continuous use of pravastatin until the onset of adverse events, including side effects (ascertained through self-report at each study visit), kidney condition (chronic kidney disease, transplant, or dialysis identified via self-report and confirmed by medical records), or another lipid-lowering treatment being started; the usual care strategy allowed for the initiation of statin therapy at any time, under the assumption that it was clinically indicated. The use of dynamic treatment strategies, under which treatment with pravastatin depends on an individual’s evolving characteristics, requires the following assumptions: (1) sufficient common causes of adherence (and loss to follow-up) and death are measured and modeled to control for time-varying confounding, (2) all types of individuals must have the possibility of following each treatment strategy, and (3) the causal contrast is clearly specified so that the strategies can be identified in the data and reproduced; see Supplemental Methods for more details on sequential exchangeability, positivity, and consistency.

We defined 3 alternative effects based on clinically relevant treatment strategies and availability of data: (1) pravastatin—take at least 80% of pravastatin, usual care—same as the original; (2) pravastatin—same as the original, usual care—do not start lipid-lowering therapy unless total cholesterol ≥240 mg/dL (LDL-C was not available for most individuals); and (3) pravastatin—take treatment until an adverse event, usual care—never initiate lipid-lowering therapy. Defining treatment strategies requires careful consideration of clinical relevance and usefulness of the causal quantity being estimated; stricter strategies, which prevent individuals assigned to usual care from initiating statin therapy, may not be applicable to real-world settings. Broader strategies that allow initiation or discontinuation of study treatments reflect per-protocol effects that are more similar to the intention-to-treat effect, which ignores post-assignment decisions.

### Intention-to-treat analysis

To estimate the intention-to-treat effect, we compared the risks (cumulative incidence proportions accounting for censoring) in each group via ratios and differences. We model the discrete-time hazards via a pooled logistic regression model that included visit (modeled using a restricted cubic spline with internal knots at 33rd and 66th percentiles), randomization group, and a product term between visit and randomization group, which allowed the HR to change over time. We then estimated risk with the predicted values of this model as previously described.13 For comparison with published results, we also estimated the HR averaged over 5 years of follow-up by fitting the same model without the product term.14 To obtain 95% CIs, we used nonparametric bootstrapping (with 500 resamples) for the risk, risk difference, risk ratio, and HR.

### Per-protocol analysis

To estimate per-protocol effects, we (1) censored individuals when they deviated from their assigned treatment strategy and (2) we adjusted for risk factors associated with adherence via inverse probability weighting to account for potential selection bias introduced by this censoring.15 We also used inverse probability weighting to adjust for potential selection bias from loss to follow-up after censoring individuals who had more than 2 years between study visits. Inverse probability weighting can handle the treatment-confounder feedback that is expected to arise because some time-varying confounders are affected by prior treatment decisions. Causal diagrams and detailed descriptions of methods for per-protocol analyses are available in a previously published work.16

We modeled the treatment non-adherence and loss to follow-up censoring mechanisms separately and included known risk factors for cardiovascular disease, specifically, age, sex, education, race, hypertensive treatment, weight, and diabetes measured at baseline, in addition to systolic and diastolic blood pressure (average of 2 measurements), total cholesterol, daily aspirin use (yes, no), oral estrogen use (yes, no), smoking (current, past, or never), healthcare utilization (count of doctor and hospital visits since the last study visit), coronary artery bypass graft (CABG), percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA), and other revascularization procedures, measured throughout follow-up. The inverse probability weight at each timepoint was the product of the treatment and loss to follow-up weights. Weights were truncated at their 99th percentile to limit the influence of outliers (see Supplemental Methods for more details).

We conducted subgroup analyses by sex (self-reported male and female) and age group (55–64 years, 65–74 years, and 75+ years), as well as among individuals without a history of cardiovascular disease, overall and by sex. Figure S1 describes the timing of data collection. Baseline information was missing on education for 524 participants, on weight for 13 participants, and on total cholesterol for 77 participants; we restricted the analysis to those with complete baseline data. Data on pravastatin, other medications, and comorbidities were carried forward up until the next available measurement. We estimated the 5 year risk, risk difference, risk ratio, and average HR using pooled logistic regression models, similar to those described above, except estimated with weights.

### Sensitivity analyses

We also explored the sensitivity of our estimates to missing data and residual confounding from truncating weights: we categorized continuous variables and used a missing indicator for data unavailable at baseline to retain the full sample, we redefined loss to follow-up from more than 2 years between visits to missing >1 consecutive visits and applied inverse probability of censoring weights, and we ran the primary analysis without truncating the weights.

## Results

Of 9741 individuals with complete baseline data, 4866 were randomized to pravastatin and 4875 to usual care (Figure 1). Baseline characteristics by randomization group, summarized in Table 1, were almost identical to those originally reported. Participants’ mean age was 66 years, 52% were male, 42% were non-Hispanic White, 32% used daily aspirin, and 90% used an antihypertensive medication. Mean BMI was 30 kg/m2 and mean total cholesterol was 224 mg/dL. After 5 years of follow-up, there were 537 deaths and 333 losses to follow-up in the group assigned to the pravastatin strategy, and 538 deaths and 400 losses to follow-up in the group assigned to the usual care strategy. The proportion of loss to follow-up at 5 years was greater for those randomized to the usual care strategy.

### Intention-to-treat effect estimates

The intention-to-treat HR for death comparing pravastatin and usual care was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.89–1.11) (Table S1) in the entire sample (same as reported previously)3 and 0.96 (95% CI, 0.85–1.08) in the subset of individuals with complete baseline data.

The 5 year risk of death also matched those previously reported; the 5 year risk difference and risk ratio were −0.6% (95% CI, −2.0 to 0.8) and 0.95 (95% CI, 0.85–1.06), respectively, for assignment to pravastatin vs usual care strategies (Table 2). The risk curves remained close for the duration of follow-up, crossing multiple times (Figure S2).

### Per-protocol effect estimates

Figure S3A displays the adherence patterns in the groups assigned to pravastatin and usual care based on the treatment strategies defined in the original ALLHAT-LLT protocol. In the group assigned to pravastatin, 66% of individuals remained adherent by year 5. In the group assigned to usual care, all individuals were adherent, by definition of this strategy. Table S2 shows the associations of baseline and time-varying characteristics with treatment adherence, and Table S3 shows associations with loss to follow-up. The combined treatment and loss to follow-up weights had a mean of 1.2 with a range from 0 to 86. After truncating at the 99th percentile, the weights had a mean of 1.2 and ranged from 0 to 3 (Figure S4A and B).

The 5 year risk difference and risk ratio estimates comparing adherence to pravastatin vs usual care strategies were −2.9% (95% CI, −4.6 to −1.2) and 0.79 (95% CI, 0.69–0.91) for death and −3.3% (95% CI, −6.8 to 0.5) and 0.83 (95% CI, 0.68–1.03) for MACEs. Risk curves for death diverged near year 4 (Figure 2A), and those for MACEs overlapped for the duration of follow-up (Figure 2B). The HRs were consistent with the 5 year risk ratios for death and MACEs (Table S1).

### Subgroup analyses

Risk ratios and risk differences for death and MACEs by subgroup are presented in Figure 3. Risk ratios for death were similar for male and female. Risk ratios for MACEs were closer to null for younger age groups, but 95% CIs were wide (Table S4).

### Secondary analyses

Changing the definitions of the pravastatin and usual care treatment strategies did not substantially change findings for death or MACEs (Table 2). As expected by construction of our alternative treatment strategies, adherence decreased when requiring ≥80% adherence to the study drug (58%), when allowing lipid-lowering treatments in the usual care arm only when total cholesterol exceeded 240 mg/dL (86%), and when prohibiting lipid-lowering treatment under any circumstances in the usual care arm (73%) and only allowing individuals in the pravastatin arm to discontinue in the presence of adverse events (65%) (Figure S4B–D). Censoring after more than 1 missed visit and using the missing indicator method also did not substantially change findings for death or MACEs (Table S5, Figures S5 and S6).

The 5 year risk ratios and risk differences per-protocol effect estimates were similar when we did not truncate the weights.

## Discussion

After defining treatment strategies compatible with the ALLHAT-LLT protocol and clinical care recommendations, we estimated that, compared with usual care, full adherence to the pravastatin strategy reduced the risk of death by 21%, and that reductions ranging from 9% to 31% were highly compatible with the data, under conventional statistical criteria. In contrast, when considering assignment to pravastatin, effects ranging from a 15% reduction to a 6% increase in risk were highly compatible with the data.

Our per-protocol estimates are compatible with meta-analyses of statin trials that found 10%-20% relative reductions in the risk of death with statin treatment compared with placebo.1,2,17 While the meta-analyses included trials that were analyzed under the intention-to-treat principle, the said trials were not pragmatic and had higher adherence than what was observed in ALLHAT-LLT, arguably rendering the meta-analyses results more comparable to our per-protocol estimates. The intention-to-treat approach is less attractive for pragmatic trials like ALLHAT-LLT. Some pragmatic trials do not implement measures to promote adherence to the protocol, which may allow for substantial deviations from the assigned treatment strategies.11 It is then possible, as our results suggest was the case in ALLHAT-LLT, that the effect of being assigned to pravastatin compared to usual care without statins is attenuated because of low adherence, but the effect under full adherence is more protective. Therefore, when there are opportunities to improve adherence, both the effect of assignment (the intention-to-treat effect) and the effect under full adherence (the per-protocol effect) are of interest to patients and clinicians.

Previous interpretations of the ALLHAT-LLT findings have suggested that the high frequency of lipid-lowering therapy initiation among those assigned to usual care may be responsible for the attenuated ITT effect.18–21 In contrast, we found a benefit of pravastatin across all clinically relevant treatment strategies we examined. As we made the usual care strategies more tolerant of statin initiation, that is, never allowing statin initiation for any reason, then only when total cholesterol exceeded 240 mg/dL, and finally, always allowing it, the estimated risk of death in the usual care group decreased. However, even under the strategy that allowed statin initiation for any reason in primary analyses, which under full adherence was equivalent to assignment to usual care, the estimated risk of death in the usual care group was higher than the risk in the pravastatin group under full adherence, that is, there were still benefits of pravastatin. These results demonstrate that accounting for non-adherence to the pravastatin treatment strategy was sufficient to show benefits of the medication when compared to the usual care treatment assignment, which reflected the natural initiation of statins, and to the usual care strategy under full adherence, in which statin initiation was tolerated only under certain circumstances.

Describing and adjusting for predictors of adherence is challenging when studying sustained, dynamic treatment strategies.22,23 Some dynamic strategies allow individuals to discontinue their assigned study medication when they develop pre-specified contraindications. The analysis, therefore, requires not only clearly defining treatment strategies but also sufficient data to evaluate whether a discontinuation is considered a deviation. Simply quantifying the proportion of individuals who initiated or discontinued the study drug overlooks important nuances in clinical circumstances and appropriate care of patients. Further, the analysis needs to adjust for time-varying prognostic factors that predict adherence, generally via inverse probability weighting or other g-methods.24–26 When designing pragmatic trials, per-protocol estimands should be incorporated a priori to enable the collection of relevant covariates, including prognostic factors that may predict adherence to treatment. This can facilitate a valid estimation of the effects of sustained treatment strategies.

Our work has several limitations. Although LDL-C is more frequently used than total cholesterol to prescribe lipid-lowering therapy, we used total cholesterol as an adjustment variable and part of the usual care treatment strategy (ie, initiation when cholesterol ≥ 240 mg/dL) since LDL-C, HDL-C, and triglycerides were only collected among a 10% subsample when this study was initiated in 1994. Given the high correlation between LDL-C and total cholesterol (both from reported literature and within our sample),27,28 we used total cholesterol in lieu of imputing missing LDL-C measurements. We adjusted for post-randomization risk factors related to adherence using inverse probability weighting, which requires that the measured variables are sufficient to adjust for differences between individuals who do and do not adhere to the treatment strategy, that there are no patterns of the measured variables that render adherence impossible, and that models for the probability of treatment are correctly specified. Finally, our results from the primary analysis reflect what would have been observed had there been perfect adherence to pravastatin when clinically warranted to the extent that we could map the pravastatin treatment strategy, which allowed individuals to discontinue after an adverse event or initiation of another lipid-lowering medication, to available data. If data on contraindications were missing, then some discontinuations may have been misclassified as deviations.

In conclusion, over 20 years after the initial publication of the ALLHAT-LLT results and ensuing controversy, we defined treatment strategies based on the trial protocol and estimated that, under full adherence to them, pravastatin strategies reduced the 5 year risk of death compared to usual care strategies. Our per-protocol estimates, which were estimated using g-methods and are valid under explicit identifiability assumptions, complement the original ITT estimates from the trial.
